claim: SlinkyProject's slurm-operator runs Slurm control-plane and worker daemons (slurmctld, slurmdbd, slurmd, slurmrestd) themselves as real Kubernetes pods via CRDs, the inverse integration direction from interLink/virtual-kubelet (which makes external Slurm jobs masquerade as virtual K8s pods).
stance_target: alternative strategies for making Slurm-hosted inference reachable by a stock InferencePool/router without customizing the router
quoted_support: Slinky slurm-operator represents each Slurm component (slurmctld for scheduling, slurmdbd for accounting, slurmd for compute workers, slurmrestd for API access) as a Kubernetes Custom Resource Definition (CRD).

claim: Because Slinky's slurmd workers run as genuine Kubernetes pods, they receive normal pod IPs and Service/EndpointSlice membership, meaning they would be selectable by a stock, unmodified InferencePool label selector -- an alternative to customizing the router to reach non-pod backends is to make the non-native compute (Slurm) itself run as native pods.
stance_target: there exists a non-router-customization path to reach Slurm-hosted compute from InferencePool
scope_conditions: inference derived from Slinky's pod-native architecture; not a claim the source makes about InferencePool specifically
quoted_support: Slinky slurm-operator represents each Slurm component... as a Kubernetes Custom Resource Definition (CRD)... managing their lifecycle as pods.

claim: NVIDIA reports Slinky slurm-operator running in production across clusters scaling to over 8,000 GPUs and 1,000+ worker nodes for LLM training and multinode inference, with NCCL all-reduce/all-gather GPU communication benchmarks matching noncontainerized Slurm performance.
stance_target: Slinky slurm-operator is production-viable at scale for GPU/LLM workloads
quoted_support: NVIDIA runs Slinky slurm-operator in production across multiple clusters, with some deployments scaling to over 8,000 GPUs. These clusters run large-scale LLM training and multinode inference workloads daily.

claim: Slinky's slurm-operator currently assumes one worker pod per node, which over-provisions resources for workloads that are exclusively single-node Slurm jobs; the companion slurm-bridge project is suggested as a lighter-weight alternative for that case.
stance_target: limitations of the Slinky slurm-operator approach
quoted_support: One constraint to be aware of: Slinky's slurm-operator currently assumes one worker pod per node. If your workloads are exclusively single-node Slurm jobs, this over-provisions relative to what you need, and a lighter-weight integration (or slurm-bridge) may be a better fit.
